data.title: How to vote in Tesla’s 2026 Annual Meeting
data.description:
Tesla’s Annual Meeting is coming up on December 3, and the company has released its voting instructions.

Shareholders can vote online, by mail, by QR code, or by phone.

All of the information will be provided in the shareholder voting materials that you will receive at your confirmed address.

If you are voting online or by phone, you will need to locate the unique control number on the insert. When prompted, you will need to enter the control number to vote.

If you are voting by QR code, you simply need to scan the QR code on the information packet, which will automatically include your control number.

If you choose to vote by mail, you will need to properly mark, sign, and date the proxy form and return your vote via the provided prepaid envelope.

Tesla’s Voluntary Retail Voting Program

Tesla has also rolled out a Voluntary Retail Voting Program that allows retail investors to give Tesla a standing instruction to vote their shares at future meetings. However, this program will start after the 2026 Annual Meeting, and shareholders can and should still vote their shares at the December 3 meeting.

How to vote if you are Canadian

If you are a Canadian who holds TSLA stock, you will need to follow your specific broker’s voting instructions. It should be noted that brokers are not able to vote uninstructed shares on director elections or Tesla executive compensation. The current deadline for the Annual Meeting is December 2 at 11:59 EST, but Canadian brokerages typically have their own deadlines, so be sure to check your specific brokerage’s details ahead of the vote.

data.title: HMD Trucking receives rest of 50 Tesla Semi truck order in Chicago
data.description:
Earlier this month we told you HMD Trucking has received its first Tesla Semi, as part of a larger 50-truck order. Now just over two weeks later the Chicago-based company taken delivery of the remaining 49 units.

The delivery count was shared by Chris Kuna on LinkedIn on Wednesday, who attended the grand opening of Tesla’s new Megacharger in Hodgkins, Illinois, where he interviewed HMD founder and CEO Henry Malukas about the trucks and charging infrastructure.

In a company blog post updated on Tuesday, HMD described the arrival of its first Semi as an important milestone.

“Taking the delivery of the first registered Tesla Semi in Illinois is a great achievement for our company, but it is the first step on the way to success. The other 49 units are coming.”

Tesla actually teased this amssive delivery of Semi trucks last week with a post on X, saying, “Hello Windy City. Chicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery.”

data.title: Mark Carney Says He Sold his Tesla For Less Than He Expected, Warns of Relying on Starlink
data.description:
Tesla was once so dominant in Canada’s electric vehicle (EV) market that Prime Minister Mark Carney joked that before 2024, EVs here “were all Teslas,” and that he even bought one himself. But when the company came up at Wednesday’s New York Times DealBook Summit, Carney had a less flattering assessment of the brand.

Host Andrew Ross Sorkin had pointed out that Tesla benefited from Canada’s lower tariff on Chinese-built EVs by bringing in cars from Shanghai. Carney acknowledged that, saying the government’s new policies cap the number of cars they can bring into the country, instead of letting the market decide how many cars they can sell.

Carney then spoke about the sale of his own Tesla. While he didn’t elaborate on which Tesla he purchased, he said it fetched less than he expected and put some of the blame on the badge.

“I don’t have it any more, sorry Elon. And I didn’t get the resale value for it that I thought I would because they don’t quite have the cachet that they used to,” Carney said.

Carney said Chinese automakers now pose the toughest competition, pointing to their fully electric models and AI features. He also called for the U.S. to work more closely with Canada and Mexico on the future of the auto industry.

Mark Carney: "…and they were all Teslas then. In fact, I bought one of them. I don’t have it anymore. Sorry, Elon, and I didn’t get the resale value for it that I thought I would because they don’t quite have the cachet that they used to." https://t.co/kmtB8hDixs

— Scott Robertson (@sarobertson_) November 18, 2026

Carney raises concerns about relying on Starlink

Sorkin also asked whether Canada was trying to avoid relying on SpaceX’s Starlink or its military counterpart, Starshield. Carney pointed to Ukraine as an example of how dependence on either system could shift from “an advantage to a huge vulnerability.”

Carney said Canada, Korea, Japan and Europe are looking at how to build backup satellite systems or ones they can control themselves. He also raised the question of which countries might pool their resources.

data.title: Tesla orders more weekend shifts at Giga Berlin after missing October production target
data.description:
Tesla has ordered more special shifts at Giga Berlin after missing its October production target, requiring employees to work up to six additional shifts before early December.

According to a report published by Handelsblatt, the extra shifts will take place on Friday nights and Saturday mornings, with the first two already scheduled. The mandatory shifts apply to employees working in vehicle production at the German factory, where Tesla is trying to increase output of the Model Y.

The first two shifts are scheduled for this Friday night and Saturday morning. The remaining four are conditional, meaning employees could be required to work additional shifts through early December.

Tesla falls short of production target

The extra shifts come after Giga Berlin failed to meet its October production target, which called for the factory to reach a weekly production rate of 7,500 vehicles.

That target was first announced in June by plant manager André Thierig, who said the factory was aiming to reach that level by mid-October.

However, Tesla fell short of that goal. On October 23, the automaker announced it had produced 7,000 Model Ys in a single week in mid-October, still 500 vehicles below its target.

Model Y demand drives production increases

Despite missing that target, the factory has continued pushing to increase production, with management citing demand for the Model Y as the reason for the latest mandatory shifts.

Giga Berlin also supplies Model Ys to Canada, along with over 30 other markets around the world. That means Canada is fighting for production allocation, translating into lengthy delivery timelines, which recently slipped as far as May 2027.

data.title: Tesla plans a Model Y without a steering wheel or pedals: Musk
data.description:
Tesla has taken plenty of heat for ending Model S and Model X production and now planning to wind down the Cybertruck to build more Cybercabs. That’s been a tough sell when the Cybercab itself has come under criticism for what buyers actually get.

With Tesla putting more factory space behind robots and robotaxis, many have wondered where cars people can buy and drive themselves fit into the company’s plans. Now Elon Musk says Tesla wants to take the steering wheel and pedals out of the Model Y, too.

Speaking Wednesday at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Musk said Tesla plans to build a fully autonomous Model Y with room for six or seven passengers, giving its Robotaxi service a bigger vehicle to run alongside the two-seat Cybercab.

Elon says @Tesla will introduce a fully autonomous version of the Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals: "It’s going to make sense for us to make cars that can seat different amounts of people. We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family. What we plan to do is have an autonomous version of the Model Y that won’t have steering wheels or pedals and would be good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people." (via NYT Dealbook Summit today)

— Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt) November 18, 2026

Why Tesla wants a bigger robotaxi

According to Musk, even though the two-seat Cybercab can cover about 90% of passenger miles, Tesla needs a robotaxi big enough for a family to cover the rest of the trips. An autonomous Model Y would give Tesla a way to serve those larger family groups while keeping the Cybercab focused on rides with one or two passengers.

Musk didn’t say whether customers will be able to buy the driverless Model Y or whether it will be reserved for Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet. Tesla launched the Cybercab earlier this year, and plans to begin deliveries to select customers for personal use only before the end of the year.

That plan has drawn its own set of criticisms, as the vehicle is essentially a paper weight and not usable unless you pay Tesla’s US$299 per month ‘Autonomy Fee,’ which even Musk himself said was too expensive.

Tesla already uses Model Ys for its Robotaxi service, but those vehicles still have conventional driving controls and can carry up to four passengers. That leaves the Model Y L with six seats across three rows as the layout for the driverless version of the electric SUV.

Where do consumer cars fit in Tesla’s plans?

A six or seven-seat Model Y would solve an obvious problem for Tesla’s Robotaxi service. If you’re travelling with the whole family, a two-seat Cybercab won’t get everyone there in one ride. For people who want to buy a Tesla they can drive themselves, though, Musk’s comments offer little reassurance. The company is already making room in its factories for more Cybercabs, and the latest Model Y Musk is talking about building is another robotaxi.

data.title: Judge orders Manitoba to reveal who excluded Tesla from EV rebate program
data.description:
A Manitoba judge has ordered the province to identify who decided to exclude Tesla from its EV rebate program, following an October court hearing.

According to a ruling issued last Friday, Justice Neville has given Manitoba 10 days to provide a complete record explaining who made the decision, what information they considered, and whether any documents are being withheld under privilege.

The order comes after Tesla challenged the province’s March 2025 decision to remove its vehicles from the rebate program, despite them being eligible when the program first launched.

Manitoba previously submitted six documents to the court, including budget materials and correspondence with Manitoba Public Insurance (MPI). However, the judge found those documents were not enough.

In the ruling, Justice Neville said the record “sheds no light whatsoever” on who made the decision, how it was reached, why Tesla was excluded, or whether the decision can be reviewed.

The province has argued that excluding Tesla was a government spending policy decision, rather than an administrative decision, and therefore cannot be challenged through judicial review.

However, the judge said the court cannot determine whether that argument is valid without knowing who actually made the decision.

Manitoba must now provide the records through a sworn affidavit from someone familiar with the matter, something the judge described as “an exceptional and unusual remedy.”

The dispute dates back to March 2025, when Manitoba removed Tesla and Chinese-made EVs from its rebate program. Tesla filed its legal challenge in June 2026.

The program currently offers $4,000 for eligible new EVs and $2,500 for used EVs, with the province extending it until March 31, 2027.

While this is a small victory for Tesla, Friday’s ruling does not overturn the automaker’s exclusion or decide whether the province acted lawfully. Manitoba’s request to dismiss the lawsuit also remains outstanding, and Tesla vehicles are still ineligible for the rebate.

data.title: Tesla’s iPhone app switches to Google Maps in version 4.63.0
data.description:
Tesla has made a subtle change to its iPhone app with the release of version 4.63.0 on Tuesday. While the App Store release notes only mention shared login support with the Robotaxi app, the update also includes at least one undocumented change: a switch to a new mapping provider.

Until now, the iOS version of the app has always used Apple Maps, but with this latest update, Tesla has switched to Google Maps, bringing it in line with the Android version.

Depending on which layer you use in your mobile app, map or satellite, you may not even notice the difference. According to Not a Tesla App, which first spotted the change, the map tiles have a more muted, greyer look when you check the car’s location, pick a destination, or use Summon.

If you use the satellite layer, the change is may be even less noticeable depending on where you are looking as Apple Maps appears to use more recent imagery than Google, at least in this example of Burnaby, British Columbia.

Iif you frequently use Supercharger Site Maps, that’s where you’ll likely notice the biggest difference following the switch to a new map provider.

Zooming into a site used to jumped from Apple’s maps to Google’s, creating a stutter and brief period of lag. That was because the Site Maps feature, since its introduction to the mobile app earlier this year, was powered by Google. Now that Google is the sole map provider, that jump is now gone.

However, with the satellite view, Supercharger Site Maps can sometimes look awkward if they are underground.

While not a change to the mobile app, vehicle software 2026.44.1 also made a change to how Superchargers are viewed – nearby Superchargers are now clustered under one marker, but that grouping has not reached the phone app.

data.title: Tesla Drops Hint at Imminent Cybercab Launch in Dallas
data.description:
Tesla has dropped a hint that Cybercab service in Dallas could be getting closer to launch, sharing a photo on Wednesday showing the city’s skyline reflecting off the window of a Cybercab.

The image, shared by Tesla’s official Robotaxi account on X, shows the distinctive green outline of Bank of America Plaza at night. Tesla accompanied the photo with a short caption: “Just leaving this here”.

The post is a not-so-subtle sign that Cybercab rides in Dallas are about to begin. The timing lines up with comments made by Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy in October, when he said Cybercab service would launch in Dallas in November.

The post comes less than one day after Texas DMV data revealed that Tesla had registered a record 200 Cybercabs in a single day, bringing Tesla’s total Robotaxi fleet above 1,500 vehicles, with more than 700 being Cybercabs.

While a portion of those are used in Austin, the sheer volume of them means many of those registered Cybercabs are likely to be deployed in Dallas, and based on today’s post, soon.

data.title: Canada may limit where Chinese EVs can drive over security concerns
data.description:
Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon says Ottawa will review where Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) are allowed to drive amid concerns over national security. The potential restrictions come as more Chinese automakers begin importing vehicles into the country.

Speaking on Wednesday, Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon was asked whether the federal government would restrict Chinese EVs from accessing military bases and government facilities.

“that will be part of a more cross-governmental review of that matter that would involve Public Safety and other departments,” MacKinnon said. (via Global News)

When asked why Canada would allow vehicles into the country that could face restrictions on where they can drive, MacKinnon said the government is “always on the lookout for risks” associated with connected vehicles.

Concerns over the ability of Chinese vehicles to collect sensitive information have already led several of Canada’s allies to introduce restrictions of their own. Germany, the United Kingdom, Poland and Czechia have limited access to some military facilities for certain Chinese vehicles, with Poland also restricting the connection of military personnel’s work phones to the vehicles.

In October 2026, the U.S. Air Force also barred vehicles made by BYD from accessing Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan.

There have been concerns raised south of the border about Chinese EVs entering the U.S. from Canada, with U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra addressing the issue in March.

“I think those cars can come in from China, come into Canada. They’re not going to cross the border into the US,” Hoekstra said.

The review comes after the federal government lowered Canada’s tariff on Chinese EVs from 100% to 6.1% earlier this year, allowing for the import of up to 49,000 vehicles annually at the lower rate.

data.title: Tesla wants to make its own solar-grade polysilicon at US$3.1 billion Texas plant
data.description:
Tesla is considering a US$3.1 billion polysilicon refinery in Nueces County, Texas, that would give the company a U.S. source for one of the key materials used to make solar cells.

A new filing puts the proposed facility near Robstown, with construction slated to start in 2027 and commercial operations targeted for 2030.

The refinery would give Tesla a way to make one of its own raw materials for solar manufacturing. The plant would turn ultra-pure trichlorosilane into solar-grade polysilicon, which can then be used to make high-efficiency N-type solar cells.

According to Tesla’s filing, China currently accounts for more than 90% of the world’s supply of solar-grade polysilicon. (h/t: Sawyer Merritt)

The filing adds another piece to Tesla’s solar plans in Texas. As Drive Tesla reported last week, site work is already underway in Fort Bend County for Project Crystal Sun, Tesla’s proposed solar cell and panel factory.

Tesla says the Texas investment depends on a tax agreement

The US$3.1 billion proposal is just that, and nothing has been approved. The company says it will only build the refinery in Texas if it secures a deal under the state’s JETI program, which would limit the property value used to calculate local school district operating taxes.

If the project goes ahead, Tesla expects to spend most of the money in 2028 and 2029. The filing estimates construction would support an average of 1,770 jobs a year across Texas from 2027 through 2030, including about 550 directly tied to the build.

Tesla plans to hire its first 260 refinery employees in 2030 and bring that number to 515 by 2032. The filing estimates the project would generate about US$63.5 billion in economic activity across Texas through 2065, with roughly US$61 billion coming from refinery operations.
